                                  INTIAL BRIEF OF COMANCHE NATION

TO THE HONORABLE LINDA H. BRITE AND LINDA J. BURGESS,
ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

         Intervenor Comanche Nation (“Comanche Nation” or “Nation”) files its Initial Brief in

this proceeding in which Joint Applicants Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) and

LCRA Transmission Service Corporation (“LCRA”) (together, “Joint Applicants”) seek to

amend their Certificates of Convenience and Necessity (“CCN”) to construct a 765-kV

transmission line (“Bell Line” or “Project”). The Comanche Nation asks that that the

Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”) issue a Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) recommending the

Texas Public Utility Commission (“PUC” or “Commission”) require that Comanche Nation

Tribal monitors1 be present during a pre-construction cultural resources survey and during

construction of the Bell Line along the route that is ultimately approved by the PUC, that

protections be ordered for certain cultural significant trees as discussed in section G(1) below,

and that the PUC order certain provisions set forth in section G(4) below be included in an

Inadvertent Discovery Plan to be implemented during construction.

    I.       INTRODUCTION

         The Comanche Nation, or Nʉmʉnʉʉ in the Comanche language (meaning “The People”)

is known as the “Lords of the Plains.” Once part of the Shoshone Tribe, the Comanche people

migrated south from the Northern Plains in the late 1600s and early 1700s in search of a new

homeland. This homeland became known as the Comanchería, or Nu mu nuu soo ko bitu

(“Comanche land”), and is fundamental to the Comanche Nation’s culture, history, and identity.



1
 “Tribal monitors are trained Native American representatives who observe construction, infrastructure, or
environmental projects to protect cultural resources, ancestral sites, and human remains.” Comanche Nation Ex. 1,
Direct Testimony of Martina Minthorn at 12.
Comanche Nation
PUC Docket No. 59475
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
Page 4
 The Comanche controlled Comanchería during their occupation of these lands, creating an

empire that allowed them to dictate trade and diplomacy for an area that includes much of

present-day Texas.

        Comanche presence in the modern-day United States was first recorded over 250 years

ago in 1743,2 and the first land boundary treaty between the Comanche and the United States

was executed in 1838.3 The lifestyle of the Comanche is well-known within the Nation, with

Tribal members referencing five major bands that frequently traveled to follow resources, often

shown through the presence of “marker trees,” which are trees purposely shaped by Comanches

that point towards important streams, sacred sites, and burial grounds. 4 Marker trees “are living

cultural resources of ongoing spiritual and historical significance.” 5 Comanche members still use

these marker trees today to identify sites of sacred significance. 6 Given Comanche’s long-time

presence and occupation of these lands, it is unsurprising that artifacts, cultural resources, and

burial grounds are widespread across this region of Texas.

        The Texas Natural Resources Code declares that “[i]t is the public policy and in the

public interest of the State of Texas to locate, protect, and preserve all sites, objects, . . . and

locations of historical [and] archeological . . . interest, including but not limited to prehistoric

and historical American Indian or aboriginal campsites, dwellings, and habitation sites [and]

archeological sites of every character . . . .” 7 It is paramount to comply with Texas law and the

public policy interests of the State of Texas that Tribal interests, many of which overlap with the

 public interest of Texas,8 are recognized and addressed by the Commission and by proponents of

large construction projects like the Bell Line.9

         The proposed Project consists of a single-circuit 765 kV transmission line that stretches

across a significant portion of Comanchería and runs approximately 214-244 miles from

LCRA’s Big Hill Substation in West Texas to Oncor’s Bell County East Switch Station within

Bell County. Jointly developed by Oncor and LCRA, the Project is one of the most powerful

transmission lines to be built in Texas, traveling through 13 counties and some of the State’s

most sensitive historically and culturally significant landscapes.

         As an Intervenor, the Comanche Nation participated fully in this proceeding and

presented expert witnesses on Comanche cultural resources (including marker trees) and

archaeology, topographical evidence that shows the historical presence of the Comanche along

the routes under consideration for the proposed Bell Line, the significant need for collaboration

by Joint Applicants with the Comanche Nation and incorporation of Tribal monitors during the

cultural resources survey as well as construction, and the importance of developing an

Inadvertent Discovery Plan that will adequately protect Comanche cultural resources, including

human remains. The Comanche Nation’s participation occurred in spite of Joint Applicants’

failure to provide notice to the Nation regarding the proposed Project.

         The proceeding’s record reflects Joint Applicants’ failure to consult with, or even notify,

the Comanche Nation despite multiple Joint Applicant witnesses admitting that the Comanche

Nation is an “affected party” for purposes of 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B). 10 The record contains

 overwhelming evidence that demonstrates the Comanche Nation’s historical presence along the

proposed Bell Line. That presence resulted in numerous cultural resources, sacred sites, human

remains, and other sacred and significant sites all along each of the 122 proposed routes. This

history and demonstrated record of cultural significance should compel your Honors to

recommend that the Commission condition the requested amended CCN for the Project on the

mandatory integration of Comanche Tribal monitors during both the cultural resources survey

and construction phases of the Project, that the Commissioners order protections for certain

culturally significant trees as described herein, and that the Commission enumerate certain

requirements for the Project’s Inadvertent Discovery Plan in its Order as set forth below.

    II.       JURISDICTION AND DEADLINE FOR DECISION

           The Comanche Nation takes no position on this issue for purposes of this proceeding.

    III.      PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES

A. JOINT APPLICATION

           The Comanche Nation takes no position on this issue for purposes of this proceeding.

B. NOTICE

    1. Did the applicants provide notice of the joint application in accordance with 16 TAC
       § 22.52(a)(1), (2), and (3)?

           The PUC’s standardized notice requirements are insufficient to notify an affected

sovereign Tribal Nation such as the Comanche Nation. While the administrative code notice

requirements focus on mailed notice to local landowners or utility ratepayers within a certain

distance of the centerline of the transmission line, the process fails to account for the unique

federal, statutory, and sovereign rights of Tribal Nations like the Comanche Nation. A Tribal

Nation’s ancestral lands, sacred sites, and burial areas extend far beyond a Tribal Nation’s


Comanche Nation
PUC Docket No. 59475
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
Page 7
 modern day reservation, and, as testified during the proceeding, the Comanche Nation is no

exception.11 The PUC’s standard buffer-zone notice requirements fail to provide for notice to

Tribal Nations whose historic, cultural, or religious lands and properties in Texas are threatened

by a multi-mile transmission corridor across much of Central Texas.

        Indeed, the land at issue in this proceeding is ancestral Comanche land ceded by the

Nation to the United States that the Comanche occupied for nearly 175 years. 12 As the record

reflects, Comanchería encompasses most of the land at issue in this 200-plus mile project. 13

During the hearing, Joint Applicants’ witness Russell Marusak acknowledged the breadth of the

Comanche Nation’s presence as reflected on the Royce Map for Texas and Adjoining States. 14

Such historic land occupancy and corresponding rights appear in ethnographies such as the well-

known Royce Maps, rather than on tax rolls or appraisal district records. 15 These government

records, which serve as the source for buffer-zone mailed notices, fail to account for the

historical and cultural significance and Indigenous rights and interests in such lands. Moreover,

they fail to account for the policy and public interest of the State of Texas. 16

        Joint Applicants and PUC staff recognize that the Comanche Nation is an affected party.

Indeed, both Joint Applicants and PUC staff member John Poole acknowledge that the

Comanche Nation is an affected party. 17 Although the record makes clear that this is the case,

 Joint Applicants acknowledge that they provided no notice to Tribal government officials of the

Comanche Nation. This oversight occurred while Joint Applicants notified other local, state, and

federal government officials.18

           As an affected party, notice to the Nation at the time the application was filed would have

afforded the Comanche Nation more time to identify harms and impacts to its ancestral land and

more time to take action to protect such land. For example, the Nation would have been able to

consult with Mr. Marusak so that Comanche interests and concerns could be incorporated into

his initial environmental assessment. Not only would this opportunity have enhanced the

accuracy of routing recommendations, but it would also have better served the Comanche

Nation’s ability to protect its known and unknown cultural resources at the outset of the Project.

Now, with this lack of notice, the Comanche Nation seeks to participate in the next phases of the

Project: Tribal monitoring during the cultural resources survey and during project construction,

and development of the Inadvertent Discovery Plan. Given the lack of notice to the Nation as an

affected party, such a remedy is reasonable, and is both necessarily and narrowly tailored to

address the gap in notice.

       2. Did the applicants provide notice of the public meeting in accordance with 16 TAC §
          22.52(a)(4)?

       The Comanche Nation does not take a position on this issue for purposes of this
proceeding.

C. PUBLIC INPUT

       1. What were the principal concerns expressed in the questionnaire responses received
          at or after any public meetings held by the applicants regarding the proposed
          transmission facilities?

            As noted in Section B above, Joint Applicants failed to provide the Comanche Nation

notice of the Project, precluding the Nation—a directly impacted sovereign government—from

participating in the public input process. As a result, the Nation was forced to file a Proposed

List of Additional Issues to notify all parties, the ALJs, and the PUC of its highly relevant and

appropriate concerns pertaining to the Nation’s cultural and historic resource interests in the

lands at issue.19 However, as the application reflects, questionnaire respondents identified

numerous of landowner and local government concerns related to archaeological and historic

sites and the presence of cultural resources along several portions of the proposed routes,

evidencing the importance of preserving these resources not just to the Comanche Nation, but to

the local community and the Texas public.

D. NEED

           The Comanche Nation does not take a position on this issue for purposes of this

proceeding.

E. ROUTE

           While the Comanche Nation does not favor one proposed route over another, it

emphasizes that the breadth of the Project area, the scope of required ground disturbing activity,

and the Project’s direct impact on both known and unknown Comanche cultural resources

require the ALJs, and ultimately the Commission, to carefully consider the community values

and historical values in developing ordering language to approve a final route. 20 The proposed

765-kV line will travel through historically and culturally sensitive lands of the Nation regardless

of the route selected. Weighing community aesthetic and historical factors requires the

 Commission to protect such interests by ordering the inclusion of Tribal monitors during the next

phases of the Project and adopting the Inadvertent Discovery Plan provisions enumerated in

Section G(4) below.

F.       COST TO CONSUMERS

         The Comanche Nation does not take a position on this issue for purposes of this

proceeding.

G.       BEST MANAGEMENT PRACTICES

         1. Are the best management practices for construction and operating transmission
         facilities that are standard in the Commission’s electric CCN orders adequate? If
         not, what additional practices should be required for the proposed transmission
         facilities?

         The standard best management practices (“BMPs”) are inadequate for this CCN

application, and for each of the pending proceedings involving CCN applications for

transmission lines that will traverse Comanchería, because those BMPs fail to recognize and

protect the unique cultural and historic resources present throughout the entire landscape for the

Permian Basin Reliability Project.21

         First, the record reflects the inadequacy of Joint Applicants’ efforts to identify Tribal

cultural and historic resources, including those of significance to the Nation, despite the area’s

rich Comanche history. As witness Rae Lynn Schneider Reinecke points out, the initial

environmental assessment (“EA”) excludes any tribal resource category and lacks any discussion

of cultural resources for the Comanche Nation or any other Tribal Nation. 22 This omission is

particularly concerning given the breadth and duration of Commanche presence throughout the

kV routes involve distinct parties. However, the ALJs and the PUC staff can recommend standard Ordering
paragraphs applicable to CCN applications involving known Tribal ancestral land.

 Project area. Further, while current PUC practices require Joint Applicants to consult with the

Texas Historical Commission (“THC”) to obtain archaeological and historical resources for

known sites, hearing testimony revealed that Joint Applicants’ process failed to document at least

three historic sites/trinomials on the proposed routes. 23 Further, multiple Intervenor landowners

have identified Native American cultural resources on their properties. Such omissions of known

sites and identification of previously unidentified cultural resources support enhancing the

current BMPs by requiring Tribal monitors during the next phases of the Project (cultural

resources survey and construction) and requiring that the Inadvertent Discovery Plan include

certain protections listed herein.

           To that end, the Commanche Nation requests that the Commission’s Final Order impose

the following conditions or requirements on Joint Applicants. First, the Order should require

Joint Applicants to contract with Comanche Nation-approved Tribal monitors during the pre-

construction cultural resources survey. Secondly, it should require Joint Applicants to prepare, in

collaboration with the Comanche Nation Tribal Historic Preservation Officer (“Comanche

THPO”) and the THC, a robust Tribal monitoring plan for transmission line construction. Key to

this plan, the Order must specify that Joint Applicants permit Comanche Tribal monitors to be

present on-site during all construction activities to monitor ground disturbing activities for the

Project in sensitive areas where the Comanche THPO has identified a high likelihood of presence

of cultural resources. To best protect marker trees, the Order must also specify that any plan must

prohibit the removal of marker trees, red berry cedar trees (Juniperus pinchotii), or Texas

mountain laurel trees (Dermatophyllum secundiflorum) unless there is a genuine risk that they




23

Comanche Nation
PUC Docket No. 59475
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
Page 12
 may fall into or touch the power lines. Further, the Comanche Nation requests that the

Commission Order that if removal of red berry cedar or mountain laurel trees is deemed

necessary based on risk to the power lines, Joint Applicants should allow access to the

Comanche Nation to harvest those trees for cultural and ceremonial purposes, rather than

wastefully disposing of them. As the record shows, the identified species are culturally

significant to current religious and cultural customs of the Comanche Nation. 24 Lastly, the Order

should adopt the following provisions as required terms of the Inadvertent Discovery Plan:

     1. Immediate Stop-Work Protocol. Upon encountering a cultural resource or burial,
        construction shall not resume until after the resource or human remains have been
        adequately protected or avoided and, if the cultural resource or human remains are Native
        American, until after the impacted Indian tribe agrees with the treatment plan for the
        cultural resource or human remains.

     2. Immediate Notification. Upon encountering a cultural resource or human remains, Joint
        Applicants or their representative shall immediately notify both the Comanche Nation
        Tribal Chairman and the Comanche THPO.

     3. Investigation. The Comanche THPO or their designee shall be granted physical access to
        investigate an inadvertent discovery of a cultural resource or human remains in situ.

     4. NAGPRA-Compliant Human Remains Provisions. Joint Applicants and their
        representatives shall comply with the Native American Graves Protection and
        Repatriation Act, 25 U.S.C. Chapter 32.

     5. Tribal Monitors. Comanche Tribal monitors and the Comanche THPO shall be permitted
        to be on-site at the site of any inadvertent discovery.

     6. Cultural Affiliation Determination. The cultural affiliation of any inadvertent discovery
        shall be determined based on available information, including information provided by
        the Comanche Nation or other Indian tribes.

     7. Treatment and Disposition of Discovered Cultural Resources. Joint Applicants, the
        Comanche THPO, and the THC shall collaborate to develop specific provisions for the
        appropriate treatment and disposition of discovered cultural resources.

        8. Project Adjustment and Avoidance. In the event of an inadvertent discovery of a cultural
          resource or human remains, the Project route shall be adjusted within the right-of-way to
          avoid damage or destruction of the resource or remains to the maximum extent possible.

       9. Pre-Construction Training Requirements. Prior to commencing construction, Joint
          Applicants shall provide responsible parties and construction personnel with training
          regarding the cultural history of the Project area, the recognition of cultural resources,
          and the requirements of the Inadvertent Discovery Plan, including the steps to be
          followed in the event of an inadvertent discovery.

       10. Confidentiality Provisions. Any cultural resource-related information provided to Joint
           Applicants by the Comanche Nation or an agent thereof shall be treated as confidential
           and shall not be disclosed by Joint Applicants except as required by law.

       11. Dispute Resolution. The Inadvertent Discovery Plan shall include fair and equitable
           dispute resolution procedures to be followed in the event of a dispute between Joint
           Applicants and an interested party regarding implementation of the Inadvertent Discovery
           Plan.

       12. Post-Discovery Reporting. Joint Applicants, the Comanche THPO, and the THC shall
           collaborate to develop post-discovery reporting procedures.

       13. Marker Trees. Marker trees are deemed a cultural resource for purposes of the
           Inadvertent Discovery Plan.

           As demonstrated below, these requirements serve as necessary best practices for this

Project, given the vast stake that the Comanche Nation has in the Project area. Notably, these

requirements do not negatively impact costs, reliability, or timeliness of the Project.

       2. For each additional practice proposed, please address the following:

               a. What is the additional cost to design, construct and operate the proposed
                  transmission facilities, including the cost to consumers?

           The proposed BMPs regarding Tribal monitoring and the Inadvertent Discovery Plan

would not increase Project costs beyond what is already part of the Project budget. As Ms.

Cooley testified, the $1.6 billion budget for the Bell Line already accounts for cultural resource

survey costs.25 Additionally, Ms. Cooley acknowledged that the current 10%-15% contingency


25
     Tr. 232:25 233:1-8 (Cooley Cross Exam) (June 9, 2026).
Comanche Nation
PUC Docket No. 59475
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

 reserve could cover costs for Tribal monitors, should the PUC require them. 26 Furthermore, Joint

Applicants have already incurred additional expenses for the CCN application that are unrelated

to the design or construction of the Project. For example, Joint Applicants’ witness Dr. Gelmann

charges $750 an hour to review and provide testimony for this proceeding. 27 The minor expense

of Tribal monitors would not materially increase overall costs for the Bell Line.

             b. What benefit, if any, will the proposed practice provide?

        In addition to the cultural and historic benefits of Tribal monitors, inclusion of Tribal

monitors during the cultural resources survey and during construction will benefit Joint

Applicants from a cost perspective by reducing the number of construction delays caused by

inevitable inadvertent discoveries, thereby reducing costs.

        i. Cultural and Historic Benefits of Tribal Monitors

        The centuries-long presence of the Comanche across the present-day State of Texas 28 has

resulted in irreplaceable artifacts and burial grounds on and beneath lands the Bell Line will

traverse, regardless of the selected route. Each of the 122 proposed routes cuts through the heart

of Comanchería.29 Maintaining the integrity of cultural resources, such as marker trees, 30 and

preserving artifacts provide immeasurable cultural, spiritual, and educational benefits to the

Comanche Nation as well as historical and educational benefits to the public at large. 31 Indeed, it

is the stated policy for Texas to preserve such important resources for the benefit of the entire

        The heavy presence of Comanche cultural resources in the Project area was recently

confirmed by a distinguished archaeologist and member of the Comanche Nation, 34 the Nation’s

witness Mary Weahkee. Prior to the merits hearing in this matter, Ms. Weahkee walked four

different properties along the proposed routes of the Bell Line. Within that short time, Ms.

Weahkee and her son, Wayne, a Tribal member who also has Comanche cultural resources

training,35 identified a strong historical Comanche presence on those properties. 36 They found

evidence of an encampment, tools, marker trees, and burial mounds, and Ms. Weahkee is

confident, based on her findings during those site visits, that similar cultural sites and cultural

resources exist throughout the Project area.37 Ms. Weahkee’s and her son’s quick identification

of those artifacts is a direct result of their Comanche archaeology training, cultural knowledge,

and lived experiences as Comanches—valuable attributes any other contractor Joint Applicants

might retain is unlikely to possess. As Ms. Minthorn testified, “Tribal members know these

landscapes and possess traditional ecological knowledge. This Indigenous expertise cannot be

learned through institutional and professional study alone . . . .” 38 Preservation of these and the

many not-yet-discovered artifacts that could be damaged or destroyed by this Project

(particularly in the absence of the cultural resource protections the Nation requests) is imperative

 to carrying on the traditions of the Comanche Nation and maintaining Comanche traditional

        ii. Economic Benefits of Tribal Monitors

        Implementing a Tribal monitoring plan during the cultural resources survey and the

construction process will, more likely than not, ultimately reduce the costs of the Project to Joint

Applicants. It is nearly certain that construction crews will encounter Comanche artifacts and

cultural resources during their excavation process, given the historical presence of the Comanche

throughout this region of Texas.40 As noted in Mr. Rossen’s direct testimony, the cost of

construction delays due to the inevitable excavation of Tribal artifacts, and potentially human

remains or burial grounds, in the absence of Tribal monitors would likely exceed the cost of

proactive involvement of Tribal monitors in the construction process. 41

    I.       INTRODUCTION

         The Comanche Nation, or Numunuu in the Comanche language (meaning "The People")

is known as the "Lords of the Plains." Once part of the Shoshone Tribe, the Comanche people

migrated south from the Northern Plains in the late 1600s and early 1700s in search of a new

homeland . This homeland became known as the Comancheria, or Nu mu nuu soo ko bitu

("Comanche land"), and is fundamental to the Comanche Nation's culture, history, and identity.

burial grounds are widespread across this region of Texas.

Applicants from a cost perspective by reducing the number of construction delays caused by

inevitable inadvertent discoveries, thereby reducing costs.

             c. What effect, if any, will the proposed practice have on the reliability of the
                transmission system?

        An Order that mandates Tribal monitors during the next phases of the Proj ect and as a

condition of the CCN will not have any impact on the reliability of the transmission system

because the Tribal monitor role has no bearing or impact on the integrity of the transmission

system. Tribal monitors observe, document, and provide advice and recommendations-they do

not affect the integrity of construction or operation of a project.

             d. What effect, if any, will the proposed practice have on the design,
                construction, or operation of the proposed transmission facilities?

        An Order that requires Joint Applicants to engage Tribal monitors would have minimal

impact on construction and no impact on the design or operation ofthe proposed transmission

facilities. Joint Applicants have already committed to and budgeted for a cultural resources

survey and have already agreed to coordinate with the THC. The additional conditions the

Nation requests enhance the current practices by adding Comanche Nation experts to the process.

The only BMP recommended herein that could temporarily halt construction is the requirement

to stop ground disturbing activities upon the discovery of cultural resources or human remains.

However, this requirement is already included in PUC staff's recommendations to the

Commission.43
